claims.text: Scale imbalance can cause smaller targets to be underrepresented when labeled data are extremely limited, potentially degrading small-target pseudo-labels and accumulating errors.
CGS uses a teacher–student framework with weak-to-strong consistency, a general segmentation branch, and a multi-head specialized branch.
Each specialist classifies pixels into background, its designated target class, and the remaining target classes.
The branches exchange pseudo-labels through bidirectional consistency losses and use a consensus mask for an additional consistency loss.
IHED filters specialist pseudo-labels using two consistency cases: all heads predict background, or exactly one head predicts its target while the other heads predict remaining classes.
Specialist heads are discarded during inference; the method retains a single segmentation head on all three evaluated datasets.

ACDC contains scans from 100 patients and three targets, with a 7:1:2 training/validation/test split. SegTHOR contains four targets with 28/4/8 volumes in those splits. Synapse contains 30 CT scans with eight abdominal organs and an 18/12 training/test split. Input slices are resized to 224 × 224.
Experiments use three different seeds on each of the three datasets and report means and standard deviations.
On ACDC, CGS achieves DSC of 88.83±0.14% with 3 labeled scans (5%) and 89.83±0.11% with 7 labeled scans (10%), compared with FixMatch's 87.27% and 88.89%, respectively.
On SegTHOR, CGS achieves DSC of 81.74±1.29% with 3 labeled scans (10%) and 83.69±1.45% with 6 labeled scans (20%), compared with FixMatch's 79.38% and 81.94%, respectively.
On Synapse with 3 labeled volumes, CGS achieves average DSC of 60.20±0.37% and average HD95 of 61.40±1.04, compared with FixMatch's 58.33% and 80.79.
CGS does not outperform BCP on ACDC 95HD with 3 labeled scans: CGS reports 2.42±0.08 versus BCP's 1.90, where lower is better.

Training incurs additional computation: reported training cost is 3.14 GFLOPs for CGS versus 2.99 for FixMatch, while both have inference cost of 2.99 GFLOPs. With batch size 24 and teacher–student networks, CGS GPU memory rises from 7.13 GB for 3 classes to 10.62 GB for 8 classes.
The authors state that IHED and cross-branch consistency depend on specialized segmentation heads, preventing independent ablation experiments for these components without that foundation.
The authors claim, to the best of their knowledge, the first investigation of scale imbalance in multi-target semi-supervised medical image segmentation.

The proposed contributions include collaborative generalist–specialist training without additional inference parameters, IHED for pseudo-label refinement, and bidirectional and consensus-based consistency losses.
